pairs.rationale: Both openings ground Paul's apostleship in God's will. Sosthenes is the brother in this address; Timothy is the brother in the other. The co-senders remain distinct.
Both addresses describe their recipients as called saints. The Roman address names those in Rome; this address names God's Corinthian Church and extends to those invoking Jesus' name everywhere.
The greetings invoke grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, giving a closely corresponding epistolary blessing.
Paul thanks God for his recipients in both letters. Here the stated ground is grace given in Christ; Romans emphasizes their faith being proclaimed throughout the world.
Both passages name abundance in speech and knowledge. The later appeal adds faith, earnestness and love and urges generosity; this thanksgiving attributes enrichment to Christ.

Both relate apostolic testimony to its reception among believers. Confirmation here and believing the testimony there remain different expressions; the latter also looks toward Christ's future glorification.
Both describe expectation directed toward the Lord Jesus Christ. Philippians names awaiting a Savior from heaven; Corinthians also speaks of gifts while awaiting His revelation.
Both connect preservation free from blame with the Lord Jesus Christ's coming or day. Thessalonians' prayer specifies spirit, soul and body; that list is not inserted into Corinthians.
Both affirm the faithfulness of the God who calls. Corinthians specifies fellowship with His Son; Thessalonians assures that the One calling will act.
Both appeals seek shared thought and unity. Philippians also stresses shared love and soul; Corinthians explicitly rejects divisions and calls for agreement in judgment.
The later argument calls jealousy and quarrels evidence of fleshly conduct, clarifying the quarrels reported here. It does not identify Chloe's people beyond this report.
The later argument repeats the Paul and Apollos party slogans. The present list also includes Cephas and Christ; those additional slogans are not silently added to the later verse.
Romans identifies baptism with Christ Jesus and His death, illuminating Paul's rhetorical rejection of baptism into Paul's name. It does not supply a baptismal transcript for each Corinthian.

Acts names Crispus at Corinth and reports his household's belief alongside many Corinthians believing and being baptized. It does not say in this verse that Paul baptized every named person or identify this Gaius.
Baptism into Christ Jesus in Romans provides the positive reference point for Paul's rejection of the claim that recipients were baptized into his own name.
The later passage identifies Stephanas's household as Achaia's firstfruits devoted to service, giving a particular internal connection to the household Paul remembers baptizing.
The later description contrasts persuasive wisdom with Spirit and power, explaining the concern about wisdom of speech here. Paul's mission emphasis is not a denial that he performed baptisms.
Both describe the saving proclamation as God's power. Corinthians contrasts responses to the word of the cross; Romans describes the good news as power for salvation to everyone believing.

The citation corresponds to Isaiah's destruction of the wise people's wisdom and concealment of the discerning people's discernment. Actual supplied wording is retained rather than making both clauses mechanically identical.
The later assertion that this world's wisdom is foolishness with God directly develops the present question about God making worldly wisdom foolish.

Both reverse expectations about human wisdom and divine disclosure. Jesus thanks the Father for revealing to infants; Paul describes salvation through believing the proclamation, not an identical audience or scene.
The scribes and Pharisees' request for a sign illustrates the sign-seeking side of Paul's contrast. It does not establish that every Jewish person made that request or address Greek wisdom-seeking.
Both connect the cross with a stumbling block. Galatians discusses the offense in relation to circumcision preaching; Corinthians distinguishes Jewish and Gentile reactions to Christ crucified.
Both locate divine wisdom in Christ. Colossians speaks of wisdom and knowledge's treasures hidden in Him; Corinthians also calls Christ God's power and names Jews and Greeks among those called.
The later comparison of Christ's crucifixion in weakness and life by God's power illuminates the weakness/power reversal. It does not call God actually deficient in wisdom or strength.
God's choice of the world's poor to be rich in faith parallels the calling that includes few socially powerful or noble. Neither passage says every believer has the same economic position.

The psalm's praise established through infants against adversaries offers a particular weakness-to-strength reversal. Corinthians applies God's choice more broadly; the groups and images remain distinct.
The lowering of the powerful and raising of the lowly corresponds to God's choice of despised and lowborn things. Luke's throne image does not define Paul's things that are not as a creation formula.
Both exclude human boasting in relation to God's saving action. Ephesians speaks of grace, faith and gift; Corinthians reaches the no-boasting conclusion through God's unexpected choices.

Christ as wisdom from God corresponds to the treasures of wisdom and knowledge in Him. The additional righteousness, sanctification and redemption terms here are not attributed verbatim to Colossians.

Jeremiah rejects boasting in wisdom, strength and wealth and directs boasting toward understanding and knowing the Lord. Paul condenses this into boasting in the Lord; Greek-based identities 9:22–23 are preserved.

Both distinguish Paul's speech from the substance of his ministry. The later letter concedes unskilled speech while denying deficient knowledge; Corinthians here says mystery of God, without substituting testimony.
Paul's resolve to center proclamation on Jesus Christ crucified corresponds to his refusal to boast except in the Lord Jesus Christ's cross. Resolve and boasting are related but distinct statements.

The Lord's encouragement not to fear during Paul's Corinthian ministry provides a specific narrative comparison for weakness, fear and trembling. No unreported psychological cause or exact occasion is supplied.
Both contrast proclamation merely in words with power and the Holy Spirit. The Spirit's demonstration here is not expanded into particular signs absent from the retained passages.
Both reserve the decisive power to God rather than human agents. The later passage uses treasure in earthen vessels; the present statement applies the contrast to the basis of faith.
Wisdom spoken among the mature corresponds to solid food for the mature with trained discernment. Hebrews' food image does not supply the identity of the rulers mentioned here.
Both speak of a divine mystery hidden across the ages. Corinthians emphasizes wisdom appointed beforehand for our glory; Ephesians describes disclosure of the mystery's stewardship in God.

Acts also attributes ignorance to the people and their rulers in Jesus' rejection. Paul specifically connects failure to know divine wisdom with crucifying the Lord of glory; ignorance is not made acquittal.

The unseen/unheard divine works correspond to Paul's citation. Isaiah names works for those awaiting mercy; Corinthians adds the human-heart clause and speaks of preparation for those loving God. These differences are retained.
Both associate the Spirit with disclosure of divine truth. John's promise of guidance into truth and Corinthians' searching of God's depths are not a grant of unrestricted knowledge to every reader.
Romans joins the searching of hearts with knowledge of the Spirit's mind. Corinthians contrasts human self-knowledge and God's Spirit's knowledge, without excluding God's knowledge of human hearts.
Both describe receiving a Spirit whose origin and character differ from an opposed condition. Romans contrasts slavery and adoption; Corinthians contrasts the world's spirit with the Spirit from God.

The Holy Spirit's teaching in John corresponds to words taught by the Spirit here. The supplied explaining spiritual things to spiritual people wording is retained without replacing it with another translation.

The world's inability to receive or know the Spirit of truth parallels the natural person's nonreception of the Spirit's things. The descriptions are not used to declare every individual's condition irreversible.

The contrast with the natural person's inability to discern spiritually explains the spiritual person's discernment. It does not make the spiritual person immune to the Church's discipline elsewhere in the letter.

The question about knowing the Lord's mind corresponds to Isaiah's question about His mind and counsel. Paul's concluding possession of Christ's mind remains an additional statement, not an inserted Isaiah clause.
Both use infancy to diagnose limited readiness for mature instruction. Hebrews speaks of inexperience in the word of righteousness; Corinthians explicitly contrasts spiritual and fleshly people.
Both contrast milk with solid food according to the hearers' readiness. The parallel concerns instruction and maturity, without assigning a precise menu of doctrines to either image.
Jealousy and quarrels in the fleshly diagnosis correspond to the flesh's works in Galatians. The lists have different contents and the Corinthian report is not evidence for every listed vice.
The earlier faction list supplies the Paul and Apollos slogans repeated here. Cephas and Christ also appear in the earlier list, but not in this two-example repetition.
Both subordinate the ministers to the Lord: servants through whom people believed here, and servants for Jesus' sake while proclaiming Christ as Lord there.

Apollos's move toward Achaia and help to those who believed supplies a particular ministry comparison for watering. Acts does not itself call his work watering or identify every Corinthian contribution.

Jesus' apart-from-Me-you-can-do-nothing saying corresponds to dependence on God's action rather than the workers' independent importance. Vine and planting images retain their different actors and settings.
The assurance that labor in the Lord is not empty corresponds to the promised wages according to labor. The latter does not specify a wage scale or erase the workers' unity here.
Both picture the believing community as God's construction. Ephesians develops the building toward a dwelling in the Spirit; Corinthians also uses the cultivated-field image for the same audience.

Both use foundation/building language for gospel ministry. Romans describes Paul's ambition not to build on another's foundation; Corinthians describes his founding work and another person's building.

Christ is central to both construction images. Corinthians calls Him the foundation; Ephesians names apostles and prophets as foundation with Christ as cornerstone. Those architectural descriptions remain distinct.

The following fire-test statement explains why the builder's listed materials matter: the quality of each person's work will be disclosed. It does not assign a fixed allegorical identity to each material.
Both use testing by fire in relation to value. Peter compares tested faith with perishable gold; Paul tests the character of work on a foundation. The tested objects are not made identical.

Both connect ministerial work with a reward. The later passage distinguishes voluntary service and entrusted stewardship; it does not identify every surviving building material or calculate the reward.

Rescue from fire in Jude offers a related salvation-through-danger image. The people, danger and instructions differ; neither passage is used to invent an unstated sequence of postmortem purification.
The community as God's dwelling in the Spirit corresponds to the plural audience as God's temple with God's Spirit dwelling among them. The corporate address is preserved.
Both call the believing community God's temple and connect it to God's presence. Corinthians here adds the threat against destroying that holy temple; the other passage does not repeat that threat.

The earlier choice of foolish things to shame the wise explains the reversal in becoming foolish to become wise. The instruction concerns claimed wisdom in this age, not rejection of all understanding.

Job's speaker says God catches the wise in their understanding; Paul's citation says in their craftiness. The close correspondence retains the different supplied wording and the original speaker's setting.
The psalm's knowledge of human reasonings as futile corresponds to Paul's wording about the wise people's reasonings. The narrower wise description and Greek Psalm93 identity are preserved.
Boasting in the Lord in the earlier conclusion contrasts with boasting in human beings here. The later all-things-are-yours argument is not substituted for Jeremiah's wording.
Both catalogues mention death, life, present and coming things. Romans denies their power to separate from God's love; Corinthians includes them among what belongs to the addressed believers.
Belonging to Christ in both passages grounds the audience's identity. Galatians develops Abrahamic descent and inheritance; Corinthians concludes its argument with Christ's relation to God.

Both describe ministry as entrusted stewardship connected with God's message or mystery. Colossians speaks of a stewardship given for the recipients; Corinthians instructs how to regard the ministers.

The faithful and prudent steward in Jesus' question illustrates the fidelity required of stewards. The household-food responsibility is Luke's image, not a literal description of every apostolic assignment.

Both subordinate human assessment to the servant's Lord. Paul's relative disregard for a human examination here does not abolish all communal accountability or claim that every assessment is forbidden.

The psalm's denial that anyone living will be justified before God helps distinguish Paul's clear conscience from the Lord's verdict. The psalm's prayer and Paul's self-report retain their different settings.
Both look toward God's examination of secrets through Christ. Corinthians also warns against judging before the time and speaks of revealed heart-purposes and praise from God.
The earlier Paul/Apollos faction slogans explain the named examples applied here against pride. The phrase not beyond what is written is not assigned an unprinted quotation source.
The statement that a person receives only what is given from heaven corresponds to Paul's challenge against boasting as though a received gift were self-produced.
Jesus' warnings to the rich and full provide a related reversal of apparent satisfaction. Paul's already-rich/already-reigning language is ironic; it is not a census proving every Corinthian wealthy.
Both describe suffering displayed publicly before others. Hebrews' spectacle of reproaches and afflictions does not identify the same incident or repeat Paul's explicit angels-and-humans audience.
Both passages ironically address people as wise while contrasting apostolic foolishness. Neither ironic description is turned into an uncomplicated endorsement of the audience's wisdom.
The later catalogue also names hunger, thirst and inadequate clothing. The catalogues overlap without requiring every hardship to belong to one journey or incident.
Paul's statement that his hands supplied his own and his companions' needs provides a specific comparison for manual labor. The blessing of insulters here remains an additional feature.

Christ's nonretaliation under reviling provides a related response to abuse. Peter speaks of entrusting judgment to God; Paul's appeal under slander and refuse image are not verbatim quotations of that response.
Both describe exhortation through a father's relationship to children. The Corinthian admonition is explicitly distinguished from shaming; Thessalonians describes encouragement toward a worthy walk.
Paul also calls Onesimus a child whom he begot during imprisonment, clarifying the ministerial fatherhood image. The two passages concern different persons and circumstances.
The later appeal to imitate Paul as he imitates Christ supplies the explicit Christ-directed qualification for the present appeal to imitate him.

Both describe Timothy being sent for the recipients' spiritual strengthening. Brother/coworker there and beloved faithful child here are distinct descriptions; the missions are not identified as one event.
Both reveal attitudes about Paul's absence and presence. The later reported contrast between weighty letters and weak presence is not assumed to come from the identical speakers described here.
Both make future action conditional on the Lord's will. James's general instruction corresponds to Paul's conditional intention to visit, not a guarantee of an unalterable itinerary.
Both distinguish God's kingdom from an inadequate outward measure. Romans contrasts food and drink with righteousness, peace and joy in the Spirit; Corinthians contrasts talk and power.
Restoration in a spirit of gentleness corresponds to Paul's gentle alternative to the rod. The disciplinary metaphor is not expanded into an instruction for physical punishment.

The prohibition concerning a father's wife's nakedness supplies a specific legal background for the reported sexual relationship. It does not establish that this woman was the man's biological mother.

Both discuss a community's response to grave wrongdoing through sorrow and discipline or restoration. The later unnamed person is not asserted to be the same offender, and its call to comfort remains distinct from removal here.

Both describe Paul's bodily absence alongside spiritual presence with a community. Colossians concerns joy in their order and faith; Corinthians concerns judgment of wrongdoing, without asserting physical presence or omniscience.

Gathering in Jesus' name and His presence with the gathered community form the specific comparison. It does not make every community judgment automatically correct or identify the meetings as one event.

Both describe handing people over to Satan with a corrective or saving purpose. Timothy names Hymenaeus and Alexander and learning not to blaspheme; the Corinthian offender and destruction-of-flesh wording remain distinct.
Both use the same little-leaven/whole-lump maxim. The Corinthian context is tolerated wrongdoing, while Galatians addresses a different threat in its argument.

The instruction to sacrifice the Passover provides the ritual background for Christ our Passover having been sacrificed. The source's Christological application is not inserted into Exodus' original household directions.

Removing leaven and eating unleavened bread provide the concrete feast background. Paul applies the contrast to malice, wickedness, sincerity and truth, rather than merely repeating a seven-day ritual command.

The later clarification restricts the association instruction to someone called a brother with the stated conduct. It does not reconstruct the text or location of an otherwise unsupplied earlier letter.
Both reject departure from the world as the required response to evil. Jesus' prayer and Paul's clarification of community association have different speakers and purposes.

Both prescribe restricted association with a disobedient member. Thessalonians also requires brotherly admonition rather than treating the person as an enemy; its case is not equated with every Corinthian vice.
The following distinction assigns judgment of outsiders to God and repeats removal from the community, clarifying the inside/outside contrast of this question.
The removal formula corresponds to Deuteronomy's command to remove the wicked from among the people. Deuteronomy's witness and execution setting is not imported as a Church punishment here.

Jesus' instructions move a brother's wrongdoing toward witnesses and the Church, providing a particular comparison with seeking resolution among saints. The two passages do not specify identical legal procedures.

Both associate the holy ones or saints with judgment. Daniel describes the Ancient of Days giving judgment to the holy ones, followed by their taking possession of kingship; Paul explicitly says the saints will judge the world. The link preserves Daniel's formulation without deciding that it states the same judging action.
Both place angels within judgment's scope. Jude describes angels kept for the great day's judgment; only Corinthians here explicitly includes the addressed we in judging angels.

The next question about finding a wise person to decide a brother's case explains the concern about appointing judges for ordinary-life disputes. The rhetorical questions retain the edition's actual wording.
The search for someone within the community to resolve a brother's case corresponds to Jesus' community-directed handling of a brother's sin. No identical court structure is inferred.
Telling the Church about unresolved wrongdoing contrasts with the brother-against-brother lawsuit before unbelievers. The target does not name the particular financial or civil claim at Corinth.
Jesus' instruction about nonretaliation and yielding even a cloak in a lawsuit provides a concrete comparison for accepting wrong rather than pursuing the present conflict.
Both condemn taking advantage of or wronging a brother. Thessalonians' surrounding sexual-ethics context differs from Corinthians' lawsuits, so the offense is not assumed identical in every detail.
Both warn that conduct in a vice catalogue excludes inheritance of God's kingdom. The catalogues overlap but retain their different terms; no unprinted item is supplied to either list.
Both include drunkenness within a catalogue connected to noninheritance of God's kingdom. The other Corinthian and Galatian items remain separate rather than being treated as identical lists.

Both connect cleansing, sanctification or renewal, justification and divine saving action. Corinthians' washed-yourselves-clean wording remains distinct from Titus' statement that God saved through washing and the Spirit's renewal.

The later verse repeats the permitted/not-beneficial contrast and adds building up. The present verse additionally refuses to come under anything's authority; that clause is not silently inserted into the later wording.

Both refuse to make food the final measure of life before God. Corinthians distinguishes food/stomach from the body for the Lord; Romans defines the kingdom through righteousness, peace and joy in the Spirit.
Both connect God's raising of Jesus with future life for believers' bodies through divine power or the indwelling Spirit. The distinct formulations are retained.
Believers as members in Christ provides the bodily-membership background for the warning against joining Christ's members to a prostitute. Romans does not itself describe that sexual case.

The two-becoming-one-flesh quotation corresponds to Genesis' marriage statement. Paul applies it to joining a prostitute; that application does not turn Genesis' wife into a prostitute or equate the settings.
The prayer for believers to be one in the Father and Son provides a related image of union with the Lord. John does not repeat one spirit or erase the contrast with bodily sexual joining here.
Both direct believers away from sexual immorality. Thessalonians calls abstention God's will and sanctification; Corinthians also explains the sin's relation to one's own body.
Both describe God's Spirit dwelling in the recipients as God's temple. The present verse specifies your body and ownership; the earlier plural address belongs to the communal-building argument.

Redemption by Christ's precious blood rather than perishable silver or gold supplies a specific comparison for being bought at a price. The body-directed exhortation here is not a literal commercial invoice.

The later concession and gift language helps prevent treating the opening good-not-to-touch statement as a universal command to remain unmarried. The letter's actual quotation punctuation is retained.
Honoring marriage and keeping its bed undefiled corresponds to the concern for a spouse in the face of sexual immorality. Neither passage is turned into a command that every person must marry.

Exodus protects the stated wife's marital provision in its particular household law. Paul makes the marital obligation reciprocal between husband and wife; the different legal situations are not merged.

The husband's love for his wife as his own body offers a specific bodily comparison. Corinthians states reciprocal authority over each spouse's body, whereas Ephesians does not repeat that authority formula.

Both connect sexual self-control with practical counsel about marriage. This verse addresses temporary, mutually agreed abstention by spouses; the later advice addresses those not exercising self-control outside that arrangement.
Both distinguish counsel from command. Concession here and judgment concerning virgins there are distinct formulations;7:25 explicitly says that there is no command from the Lord.

Jesus' qualification that not all receive the saying but those to whom it is given corresponds to differing gifts concerning unmarried life. Paul is not identified as one of the eunuchs Jesus describes.
The later judgment about the widow remaining as she is corresponds to the counsel to the unmarried and widows here. It is a recommendation, without making marriage sinful.

Timothy's counsel that younger women marry provides a related recommendation of marriage. Corinthians names lack of self-control; Timothy names household responsibilities and giving the opponent no opportunity for abuse. The circumstances are not assumed identical.

Jesus' teaching on divorce and remarriage provides the Lord-saying background for the instruction not to separate or dismiss. The actual Markan wording is retained without inserting an exception clause from elsewhere.

Jesus' statement about a wife's divorce and remarriage corresponds to the concern about separation here. Corinthians explicitly provides remaining unmarried or reconciliation, which Mark does not spell out.
The next verse gives the reciprocal case of a woman with an unbelieving husband willing to remain, matching the principle while distinguishing the spouses' roles.
The preceding verse states the corresponding case for a believing brother with an unbelieving wife. Each case retains the unbelieving spouse's agreement to continue living together.

Both use holiness extending through a relationship: root and branches or first portion and dough in Romans, spouses and children here. The relationships differ; neither passage supplies automatic individual salvation for the other.
The conditional call to live peaceably with everyone corresponds to being called in peace here. Romans does not establish the marital-status consequences of an unbelieving spouse's departure.

Peter describes an unbelieving husband's possible winning through his wife's conduct. Paul's question retains uncertainty about saving a spouse rather than promising that every such spouse will believe.
Paul's teaching in every Church corresponds to his all-Churches direction here. Uniform teaching is not turned into a claim that every believer has identical social or marital circumstances.
Both resist adopting circumcision as a new requirement for their addressed believers. Galatians names the obligation of the whole law; Corinthians also tells those already circumcised not to undo it.

Both deny decisive status to circumcision or uncircumcision. Corinthians emphasizes keeping God's commandments; Galatians names faith working through love. Those conclusions are related without replacing each other's wording.
The later restatement repeats remaining in the condition of calling and expressly adds with God.

The description of receiving Onesimus as more than a slave and a beloved brother offers a specific comparison of slavery and Christian belonging. It does not explicitly narrate legal manumission or replace this verse's freedom opportunity.
Freedom joined with belonging in service to God parallels the Lord's freedperson/Christ's slave reversal. Romans contrasts sin and God; Corinthians addresses actual slave and free social conditions.
The earlier bought-at-a-price statement gives the same ownership premise with a different exhortation: glorify God in the body there, avoid human enslavement here.
This restates the instruction to remain in one's calling while adding with God. The matching wording does not remove the intervening freedom qualification.

The earlier concession/command distinction corresponds to the judgment offered here with no command from the Lord. The supplied virgins wording is preserved, without assigning an unprinted parent or fiance role.
The shortened-time and passing-world argument gives a specific internal comparison for the present-distress counsel. It does not identify an unreported historical crisis or calculate an end date.
The marriage-specific bound/released advice applies the broader remain-in-calling principle. It is not expanded into a ban on marriage contrary to the following explicit qualification.

Marriage honored in Hebrews corresponds to Paul's explicit denial that marrying is sin. Paul's warning of affliction in the flesh remains alongside that permission; Hebrews does not promise absence of hardship.
Both counsel conduct under a shortened or advancing eschatological time. Neither supplies a calendar date or an exact remaining interval, and their concrete exhortations remain distinct.

Setting thought on what is above provides a related reorientation toward earthly experiences and possessions. Corinthians' weeping, rejoicing and buying examples are not a command for indifference to people's suffering.
Both explicitly describe the world's passing away. John adds the passing of desire and the abiding of the one doing God's will; Corinthians speaks of using the world without full absorption.
The later statement of undistracted devotion to the Lord explains the aim behind concern for the Lord's affairs here. It does not deny that married believers can be devoted to the Lord.

The following comparison gives the corresponding concern of a married woman for pleasing her husband. The different descriptions of married and unmarried conditions are not themselves a declaration that marriage is sin.
The unmarried woman's and virgin's concern for the Lord corresponds to the earlier unmarried man's concern. The body's and spirit's holiness language remains specific to this verse.
The earlier explicit permission to marry supports the present assurance that the advice is for benefit rather than a noose. Relative advantages are not made a universal prohibition of marriage.
Both explicitly deny sin in marrying. The ambiguous relationship to his virgin here is preserved without supplying a father's or fiance's identity absent from the actual wording.

The following conclusion places the firm decision alongside giving in marriage and evaluates both. The stated freedom from compulsion is not replaced with a universal obligation to choose one condition.
The earlier denial that marriage is sin corresponds to saying that the one giving in marriage does well. The relative better judgment does not turn the approved alternative into wrongdoing.

Both state that a wife's marital bond lasts while the husband lives and ends at his death. Corinthians additionally limits the free choice of remarriage to in the Lord; Romans' illustration does not repeat that qualification.

Both present Paul's judgment in this counsel. The claim to have God's Spirit here is retained alongside the earlier statement of no command from the Lord, without turning judgment into a quoted dominical saying.

Marriage counsel preserves concession/command distinctions, each spouse's reciprocal obligations and differing gifts. The supplied his virgin wording is not reassigned a parent or fiance identity; Philemon does not narrate a legal manumission.1Timothy5:14 actually says younger women, and the final explanation preserves that wording.

Internal links specify a repeated argument, explanation or named household. Narrative comparisons do not identify different co-senders, unnamed offenders or missions without explicit evidence. Corporate temple language and the body/Spirit context remain distinct. No new original-language or critical-text verification is claimed.
